ml-benchmark-science.lens: Science of ML evaluation and benchmarking (leakage, splits, hidden tests, statistics, metric validity, construct validity, ceilings, documentation, freezing, Goodhart, adoption), aimed at the checked plan in plan.md

principles.name: Split by the unit that leaks
principles.plain: Rows that share a source (same paper, same formula, same duplicate file) must sit on one side of a split. A script must print a leak report that proves it.
principles.how_to_check: For each train/test or calibration/test split in the plan: is the group unit named, does a script print 'share of test rows with a sibling in train' for that unit, and is that share 0? Yes/no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: D3 freezes a list of paper IDs. But correction 17 says most of the 25.5 to 42.2 jump is unseen formulas, and correction 19 says a chemical-system holdout still leaves the test paper in training 52.4% of the time. One group key is not enough: the leak report must cover paper AND formula, and the seen/unseen breakdown must stay beside every number. D2's 'one private check that matters' (a duplicate pair on both sides of the calibration/test split) is the same principle on the X-ray side. The general claim is old (2018 in materials), so the news in N2 can only be the TE-specific numbers and the frozen list.

sources.title: Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science
sources.what_it_says: Leakage errors found in 17 fields, affecting 329 papers. Gives a taxonomy of 8 leakage types and proposes model info sheets. In one case study the claimed ML advantage vanished once leakage was fixed.

sources.title: Can machine learning identify the next high-temperature superconductor? Examining extrapolation performance for materials discovery
sources.what_it_says: Standard cross-validation overestimates performance for materials discovery. Proposes leave-one-cluster-out cross-validation and a nearest-neighbour baseline. (Publisher page returned 403; the group's own summary page was opened.)

sources.title: MD-HIT: Machine learning for materials property prediction with dataset redundancy control
sources.what_it_says: Many near-identical materials in a dataset make random splits give inflated scores. Releases a tool that thins a dataset so no two samples are closer than a threshold.

principles.name: Freeze test list and decision rule first
principles.plain: Fix the test items, a separate tuning set, and the pass/fail rule before looking at results. Log any later change with old and new numbers side by side.
principles.how_to_check: (a) Before the run, does a dated, hashed file hold the test list, a separate dev list, and the decision threshold? (b) Were all baseline settings chosen on dev only? Yes/no to each.
principles.why_it_matters_here: D1's done-test ends in a one-line verdict ('worth building' or 'bug-fix') but gives no threshold: how many differing rows must be real chemistry? The two sort categories have no written definition yet, and the sorter is the person who wants the answer. D3: the 5-neighbour vs 1-neighbour choice was already compared on test numbers (correction 17), so N2's new baseline needs a dev split cut from the training papers. Already right: N3 fixes its 'harder' bands in advance; changing the project's marker needs a dated amendment; the project itself was pre-registered on 2026-07-09.

sources.title: Pre-registration for Predictive Modeling
sources.what_it_says: Predictive modelling suffers from data-dependent choices and unintended test-set reuse. Offers a lightweight pre-registration template and is frank about its limits.

sources.title: The Ladder: A Reliable Leaderboard for Machine Learning Competitions
sources.what_it_says: Repeated scoring against one holdout lets entrants overfit it. Gives a leaderboard mechanism with guarantees under adaptive submissions.

sources.title: Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?
sources.what_it_says: Fresh test sets built by the original recipe cut accuracy by 11 to 14% on ImageNet, while model rankings held. Only a fresh set shows this.

principles.name: Intervals that respect clusters; compare paired
principles.plain: Every score gets an interval. Count independent units, not rows. Compare two tools on the same items with a paired test.
principles.how_to_check: Does the D4 function take a cluster ID and a paired flag, and does 38 vs 35 of 40 still return 'tie' when the 40 scans are clustered into 20 mixtures? Yes/no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The 40 scans are 20 mixtures, each scanned for 2 and for 8 minutes. So there are 20 independent powders, not 40. TE rows cluster by paper (12,222 rows, 3,015 papers). builds.md records that row-level intervals on clustered data were wrong in an earlier round. D4's spec does not mention clusters. The same function should be pointed at the marking rules too: 'strict off on 8 of 18, lenient off on 13 of 18' is a paired comparison on 18 items and is probably a tie.

sources.title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
sources.what_it_says: Treat test items as a sample from a larger population. Gives formulas for standard errors, for differences between two models, and for planning an eval. (Clustered standard errors are in the body of the paper; I opened the abstract page only.)

sources.title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to Testing Statistical Significance in Natural Language Processing
sources.what_it_says: Significance testing is often skipped or misused in NLP papers. Gives a simple protocol for picking the right test.

sources.title: Approximate Statistical Tests for Comparing Supervised Classification Learning Algorithms
sources.what_it_says: From memory, not opened in this run: recommends McNemar's paired test when two classifiers are scored on one shared test set.

principles.name: Size the test before building it
principles.plain: Decide the smallest difference you care about, then compute how many items you need. If you cannot get that many, say plainly that the test cannot rank tools.
principles.how_to_check: For each planned comparison: is a minimum detectable difference, and the n it needs, written down before data are run or collected? Yes/no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: L2 passes: about 385 powders for plus or minus 5 points near 50% accuracy; 470 to 780 paired powders to separate two tools 5 points apart. Not yet done for N3: the number of powders per minor-ingredient band is unknown until D6, and the under-10%-by-weight band of a 240-mixture set may give intervals near plus or minus 10 points. Not done for the 25-pair table either: it cannot rank five marking rules. It is a unit-test file, not a leaderboard of markers. N2 should resample by paper when it sizes its three-split comparison.

sources.who: Card, Henderson, Khandelwal, Jia, Mahowald, Jurafsky
sources.title: With Little Power Comes Great Responsibility
sources.what_it_says: Underpowered experiments are common in NLP. Small test sets in a popular benchmark cannot support most comparisons to the state of the art. A typical 2,000-sentence translation test set has about 75% power to detect a 1-point difference.

sources.title: Adding Error Bars to Evals
sources.what_it_says: Includes power analysis for planning an eval.

principles.name: Give the metric a signature and version
principles.plain: A score is comparable only if the scoring settings are printed with it. Ship the metric as code that emits a settings string, and store that string with every score.
principles.how_to_check: Does every stored score row carry a string naming: rule and version, tolerance, reference library and snapshot date, tool version, candidate cap, and whether 'correct' means the exact set of phases or per-phase credit? Can the 12/17/32/38 spread be fully explained by differing fields of that string? Yes/no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: This is the closest ML twin of the X-ray marking problem. Correction 1's three causes (the rule, stale stored marks, the reference library and set-up) are three signature fields. The 15 stale rows are cached scores with no version. Today's tools report in different units: one reports 'k of 40', one a phase recovery rate decided by a GPT-4 judge, a September 2026 one micro-F1. None can be compared. The week-1 table is the right first test of whether a signature alone removes the spread.

sources.title: A Call for Clarity in Reporting BLEU Scores
sources.what_it_says: The same translation metric differs by up to 1.8 points between common configurations, mostly from text pre-processing. Scores across papers are not comparable. Proposes a community-standard scheme and a tool (sacreBLEU) that enforces it.

sources.title: Automated multiphase identification and refinement in powder diffraction using mismatch-tolerant machine learning
sources.what_it_says: Scores phase recovery on 291 mineral-archive samples (79.7% vs 64.3% for Dara). A GPT-4 prompt decides whether predicted and reference structures are the same phase; it accepts alternate settings, supercells, hydration differences and defect variants.

sources.title: Scalable machine learning framework for multiphase identification from powder X-ray diffraction
sources.what_it_says: Abstract only: reports micro-F1 of 0.935 on a curated experimental set. The abstract gives no item count, matching rule or interval.

principles.name: Check the metric against expert judgment
principles.plain: A marking rule is itself a model. Test it against labels from at least two specialists working apart, and report agreement with an interval. An AI-drafted key is a draft, not ground truth.
principles.how_to_check: Is there a set of pairs labelled by 2 or more specialists independently, with their agreement reported, and is each marking rule's agreement with them given with an interval? Until then, is every figure against the AI key worded 'disagrees with the draft key'? Yes/no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: D1 labels its key 'AI-drafted, not yet reviewed' (good). L1 asks one specialist. One rater gives no agreement number, and the notes say specialists publicly disagree on ordered vs disordered crystal versions. The same issue hides in the week-1 test: 'spelling artifact vs real chemistry' is a chemistry judgment made by a newcomer plus an AI. Do two blind passes and list where they differ. The field's one published equivalence judge (a GPT-4 prompt) was not validated against people in its paper. That is both the gap and the prior art.

sources.title: Tangled up in BLEU: Reevaluating the Evaluation of Automatic Machine Translation Evaluation Metrics
sources.what_it_says: How you judge a metric against human ratings is itself fragile: outliers can mislead. Proposes checking metrics on pairwise system rankings with thresholds for the two kinds of error.

sources.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
sources.what_it_says: A strong LLM judge agreed with people over 80% of the time, the same as people with each other. It also shows position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases.

sources.title: Automated multiphase identification and refinement in powder diffraction using mismatch-tolerant machine learning
sources.what_it_says: The page describes the GPT-4 equivalence judge and visual checks of fit plots, but no validation of the judge's verdicts against specialists.

principles.name: Say what decision the score supports
principles.plain: A benchmark measures a construct: the real-world ability you care about. Name the user and the decision, then check that the items and the scoring match it.
principles.how_to_check: Does each marking preset and each exam name one user and one decision (for example 'did my synthesis make the target compound?') and say which tiers count as correct for that use? Does the sample type match that use? Yes/no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The tiered marker is the right shape, because 'correct' depends on use. A synthesis chemist may accept a different crystal form; an analyst measuring amounts may not. Weighed mixtures of bought powders are not reaction products: the marking rule moved 12 vs 32 of 40 on the first and only 1 to 3 of 20 on the second. So the exam type changes the finding. TE: relative error on a signed quantity is a weak construct; the plan adds sign accuracy and absolute error (good).

sources.title: AI and the Everything in the Whole Wide World Benchmark
sources.what_it_says: Famous benchmarks are framed as general measures of progress but have construct validity problems: they are narrow and carry hidden assumptions.

sources.title: Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks
sources.what_it_says: Review of 445 benchmarks. Finds patterns that undermine validity and gives eight recommendations, starting with defining the phenomenon being measured.

sources.title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?
sources.what_it_says: Sets four criteria for a benchmark. The abstract names the areas: dataset design, annotation reliability, size, and handling of social bias.

sources.title: Matbench Discovery: A framework to evaluate machine learning crystal stability predictions
sources.what_it_says: A materials example: a model with good regression error can still give many false positives at the decision boundary, so the metric must match the task.

principles.name: Show floor, ceiling and headroom
principles.plain: Put a trivial baseline and a best-achievable score beside every result. Build a test only where the gap between them is wider than the test's own error bar.
principles.how_to_check: Does each results table show (a) a trivial baseline, (b) a ceiling from label noise or human agreement, each with an includes/excludes line, and (c) is ceiling minus best current tool larger than the interval half-width at the planned n? Yes/no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: N4 does (a) and (b) for TE: 0.48% reading noise, 12.9% within a paper, 32.7% across papers, 15.0% answers-known ceiling, 42.2% model. The X-ray side has no ladder yet. N3 needs a floor (for example 'always name the major ingredients') and a ceiling per band (lab X-ray scans cannot see ingredients below roughly 1 to 5% by weight; a specialist on the same scans). The plan already used headroom well: the 40-scan set is saturated (38 vs 35 is a tie), and the relabelled set was dropped (random 20.1% vs perfect 21.8%). L2's sizing assumes accuracy near 50%; N3 must confirm that before any lab is asked.

sources.title: Are we fitting data or noise? Analysing the predictive power of commonly used datasets in drug-, materials-, and molecular-discovery
sources.what_it_says: NOT opened (publisher and preprint pages returned 403). From search results only: derives best-achievable scores for nine datasets from experimental error; four had published models at or past that bound; releases a Python package and web app.

sources.title: Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets Destabilize Machine Learning Benchmarks
sources.what_it_says: At least 3.3% label errors on average across 10 test sets, at least 6% in ImageNet validation. Wrong test labels can flip which model looks better.

sources.title: Mapping global dynamics of benchmark creation and saturation in artificial intelligence
sources.what_it_says: Across 3,765 benchmarks, a large share moved quickly to near-saturation.

sources.title: Dynabench: Rethinking Benchmarking in NLP
sources.what_it_says: Models top benchmarks fast yet fail simple challenge cases; proposes benchmarks that are refreshed with harder items.

principles.name: A hidden test needs rules, not just secrecy
principles.plain: Blind tests work because of governance: fresh items each round, a custodian who is not a contestant, limits on scored submissions, and published independent assessment.
principles.how_to_check: Does the L2 one-page request name each of: a custodian who does not enter; a hash of the answer key lodged before release; a cap on scored submissions; file names and headers with no recipe clues; a plan for new powders each round; what is published afterwards? Yes/no per item.
principles.why_it_matters_here: L2 lists pilot size, the file-naming rule and who holds the answers. Missing: a submission cap (repeated scoring leaks the key), a refresh plan (once answers are released the set becomes a practice exam), and the conflict if the partner lab also builds a tool that enters. One lab means a one-instrument exam; the plan says so. Public file names that spell out recipes are the X-ray version of test data posted in plain text.

sources.title: CASP home page
sources.what_it_says: Blind prediction of structures not yet public, every two years since 1994, judged by independent assessment teams, results published in a journal.

sources.title: The Ladder: A Reliable Leaderboard for Machine Learning Competitions
sources.what_it_says: Repeated submissions against one holdout corrupt a leaderboard; gives a principled fix.

sources.title: Stop Uploading Test Data in Plain Text
sources.what_it_says: Practical steps against test-set contamination: encrypt public test data and bar derivative distribution; avoid items whose answers sit online; release source context.

principles.name: Ship a datasheet with every artefact
principles.plain: Each list, key or table ships with a short sheet: source snapshot and hash, how rows were chosen, who or what made the labels, licence, known errors, and what it must not be used for.
principles.how_to_check: For each file the plan ships (tricky-pairs CSV, 499-row match table, frozen paper-ID list, number card): is there a one-page sheet with those fields, and does it say 'not a hidden test' where answers are public? Yes/no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The plan has the pieces, scattered: checksums (D0, D3), an 'AI-drafted' label column (D1), a basis-of-evidence column and neutral wording (D2), IDs only for unlicensed data. There is no common template. N5 ('four questions before trusting a materials leaderboard') overlaps existing general checklists of 46 criteria and 32 questions. N5 should map onto them and claim only the materials-specific parts.

sources.title: Datasheets for Datasets
sources.what_it_says: Every dataset should come with a sheet covering motivation, composition, collection process and recommended uses.

sources.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
sources.what_it_says: Short documents stating intended use, evaluation procedure and performance across conditions.

sources.who: Reuel, Hardy, Smith, Lamparth, Hardy, Kochenderfer
sources.title: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices
sources.what_it_says: Scores 24 benchmarks against 46 lifecycle criteria. Most do not report statistical significance and are hard to replicate. Ships a minimum-quality checklist.

sources.title: REFORMS: Reporting Standards for Machine Learning Based Science
sources.what_it_says: A 32-question checklist with guidelines, written by 19 researchers, for authors, referees and journals.

principles.name: Read the rows; keep hand-picked sets apart
principles.plain: Totals hide causes. Publish row-level tables and slice by known factors. Never quote a pass rate on hand-picked hard cases as an error rate in the wild.
principles.how_to_check: Does each headline number come with a row-level file and at least one slice named in advance? Is every figure from the tricky-pairs file worded as 'unit tests failed', not 'percent wrong'? Yes/no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The plan is strongest here: the 40-row hand sort, the seen/unseen formula breakdown, accuracy by minor-ingredient band, and the per-scan flag 'were all true ingredients in the candidate list'. The risk is wording. 'Strict wrong on 8 of 18' comes from pairs chosen to be hard. The prevalence number is the 40-row count, and that covers one tool install on one dataset.

sources.title: Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with CheckList
sources.what_it_says: Held-out accuracy hides failures. Proposes unit-test style checks: minimum functionality tests, invariance tests, and more. Users wrote twice as many tests and found almost three times as many bugs.

sources.title: Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets Destabilize Machine Learning Benchmarks
sources.what_it_says: Row-level review of test labels found errors that change conclusions drawn from totals.

principles.name: Replicate before you generalise
principles.plain: A finding about a benchmark on one dataset and one tool is local. Show it on a second independent dataset and tool, or word it as local.
principles.how_to_check: Is each headline claim in N5 shown on 2 or more independent datasets and 2 or more tools? If not, does the text say 'in our set-up'? Yes/no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The marking effect held on 1 of 2 X-ray datasets, with one local install (version 1.1.12, open reference pools capped at 80 candidates). The TE split effect is one database and formula-only models. The plan's 'do not sell 12-to-32 as field-wide' passes. N5 must keep that wording. N3 is the natural replication: re-mark its results under every rule.

sources.title: The Benchmark Lottery
sources.what_it_says: Which method looks best can change a lot just by picking different benchmark tasks.

sources.title: We Need to Talk about Standard Splits
sources.what_it_says: Rankings reproduced on the standard split did not all survive re-drawn random splits.

sources.title: Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?
sources.what_it_says: A careful replication of a test set changed absolute scores a lot but kept rankings.

principles.name: Assume the score will be gamed
principles.plain: Once a number is a target, tools drift toward what it rewards. Design the score so that vague or padded answers lose.
principles.how_to_check: Does the marker charge for extra wrong phases as well as missed ones? Does 'cannot tell' score below 'same'? Would a tool that lists more phases, or a vaguer formula, gain under any preset? Run it as a unit test. Yes/no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The lenient rule already merges different compounds (Nb2O5 with Nb12O29). Notes G23: adding a spurious phase always improves the curve fit, so X-ray tools over-answer by default. 'k of 40 correct' hides whether extra phases were charged. It also applies to the user's own project: moving its marker after seeing 0.309 vs 0.745 is the same trap, and the dated-amendment rule covers it.

sources.title: The Problem with Metrics is a Fundamental Problem for AI
sources.what_it_says: Optimising a metric invites gaming and short-term focus (Goodhart's law). Remedies: several metrics, qualitative checks alongside, and input from the people affected.

principles.name: No user, no benchmark
principles.plain: Most benchmarks are never adopted. Secure one outside user or host before building for outsiders, and make the tool trivial to run.
principles.how_to_check: Before N1 or N5 is built for others: is there one named outside tool author, benchmark host or specialist who has said they would run or host it? Yes/no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The only sure user is the user's own project; the plan says so. The notes record a metals benchmark with 3 submissions against 6,044 downloads. The BLEU-signature tool spread because it was one install, printed a signature, and tied itself to the community's existing standard. The twin here: offer the marker as an option inside an existing tool's own marking script or an existing X-ray benchmark, not as a new standalone. The plan's 'one question only you can answer' is this principle.

sources.title: Mapping global dynamics of benchmark creation and saturation in artificial intelligence
sources.what_it_says: Many of 3,765 benchmarks never found wide use.

sources.title: Reduced, Reused and Recycled: The Life of a Dataset in Machine Learning Research
sources.what_it_says: Benchmark use concentrates on fewer and fewer datasets, mostly from a small number of institutions.

sources.title: A Call for Clarity in Reporting BLEU Scores
sources.what_it_says: Adoption route: adopt the existing community scheme and ship a tool that enforces it.

Proposes two new metrics (METRe, cRMSE) and cleaned splits, including variants with mirror-image pairs.

ml-benchmark-science.notes:
IS THIS EVAL WORK? Yes. Almost every planned item is an evaluation-science item, and mostly meta-evaluation (testing the tests, not the models). Map: D1/N1 = metric validity and versioning (the sacreBLEU problem). D2 = data validity and contamination. D3/N2 = leakage and splits. D4 = error bars. D6/N3/L2 = test-set construction and hidden-test governance. N4 = ceilings. N5 = a benchmark checklist. D5/N6/L3 = label-error audit. Only D0 (file rescue) is not eval work. So checking the plan against eval principles first is a fair ask.

WHERE THE PLAN ALREADY PASSES (by my reading of plan.md): local wording of claims (P12); row-level error analysis and slices (P11); power sizing for L2 (P4); headroom used to kill two ideas (P8); 'practice exam, never hidden' for public answers (P9); AI-drafted key labelled as draft (P6); dated amendment before touching the pre-registered project (P2, P13); flag-never-fix.

WHERE IT FAILS OR IS SILENT (each is cheap to fix before starting D1):
1. D1 has no pre-written threshold for its one-line verdict and no written definition of 'spelling artifact' vs 'real chemistry'. The sorter is a newcomer plus an AI, single pass (P2, P6).
2. D4 has no cluster argument. 40 scans are 20 powders; TE rows cluster by paper (P3).
3. No metric signature is planned for stored scores, though correction 1's three causes are exactly three signature fields (P5).
4. D3/N2 have no dev split; the neighbour count was already compared on test numbers (P2). The leak report needs two keys, paper and formula (P1).
5. The X-ray side has no floor/ceiling ladder; N3 needs one per band before L2's 'near 50%' sizing is trusted (P8).
6. L2's one-pager lacks a submission cap, a refresh rule and a custodian-conflict line (P9).
7. The marker's handling of extra wrong phases and of 'cannot tell' is unspecified (P13).
8. No common datasheet template; N5 does not yet map to existing checklists (P10).
9. No outside user is named for N1/N5 (P14). The plan admits this.

PRIOR ART THE NOTES DO NOT HAVE (grep of plan.md, gaps.md, builds.md, storyline.md, glossary found no mention): sacreBLEU, CheckList, Miller 2024, Card et al., Kapoor-Narayanan, REFORMS, BetterBench, Meredig 2018 leave-one-cluster-out, MD-HIT, Crusius et al. noise bounds, Martirossyan et al. 2025 on structure-match metrics, Wei et al. 2023 / CSPBench, the Ladder, Jacovi et al., GALAXI (Sept 2026), and a 2026 TE paper that already reports a composition-wise split drop. None of these kills a planned item. Several shrink novelty claims: N2's general point is 8 years old in materials; N4 has a close cousin with a released package; D4 and N5 are implementations or specialisations of known work and should say so.

UNKNOWN / OUT OF REACH: Whether a paper-level TE leakage audit exists is still unknown (two searches, not exhaustive). Whether Crusius et al. include any TE data is unknown (pages returned 403). GALAXI's matching rule and test size are unknown (abstract only). How the Dara paper's own marking script decides 'correct' is unknown from the abstract page.

SOURCING HONESTY: opened=true means I opened that URL in this run, usually the arXiv abstract page, not the full paper. Where a detail lives only in a paper's body (for example Miller's clustered standard errors) I say so. opened=false items: Dietterich 1998, Crusius et al. 2025, the Materials and Design TE paper, MatFold, Codabench, the IUCr round robins, XRDBench. For these I relied on search snippets, the notes, or memory, as stated per item. Publisher pages at RSC, Nature, Springer, ChemRxiv and ScienceDirect refused access (403 or login redirect). validity-and-strategy.notes:
DIRECT ANSWER TO THE USER'S QUESTION. Yes, this is evaluation work. Almost every planned item is an eval. About five of them (D1 tricky-pairs key, D4 tie function, N1 tiered marker, N4 noise ladder, N5 'four questions' note) are one level further up: tools and commentary about how exams are marked. That is evaluation of evaluation. And yes, it is worth checking principles before the next step. The check below changes the order of work more than the content.

VERDICT UNDER THIS LENS: right direction, mis-sequenced, with real drift risk. (1) 'Evaluation data before a training corpus' was a deliberate earlier decision and it survives validity theory. (2) But the weight of the plan has slid from evaluation DATA (trusted measured test items, which is curation, the user's stated focus) to evaluation TOOLING and notes, because tooling is what can be done at a desk. The curation items (D2 match table, D5 corrections, N6 suspect list, D3 frozen DOI list) were demoted to 'courtesy'. (3) Most desk items polish internal validity (marking, ties, splits, noise). The plan's own numbers say the signal is in external validity: on 20 real reaction products the marking rule moves 1 to 3 of 20 while the tool gap is 11 to 13 of 20. (4) The only certain user is the user's own project. No outside decider is named for any item. (5) The step that decides the fork (will one diffraction specialist engage) sits after about two weeks of desk work. It should run in parallel from day one. It needs the user's yes and the user sends it.

WHAT MAY BE OUT OF REACH. The dominant bottleneck under this lens is fresh, hidden, measured test items from real reactions, with an answer key made independently of the tools. That needs a lab and someone who holds the answers for years. A small outside team may not be able to get this. The honest small version is a one-off blind check with one lab, labelled as such. For thermoelectric (TE) data the values are already public, so any benchmark is a practice exam. The plan already says this; keep saying it.

NEW FACTS FOUND THIS RUN (not in plan.md or gaps.md). (a) The Dara paper (arXiv 2510.19667, HTML version) reports its own weighed-mixture test as 10 binary plus 10 ternary mixtures at two scan times: Dara 18/20 and 20/20, the commercial tool 16/20 and 18/20. So the best tool is already at ceiling on the 8-minute scans; headroom exists only in the 2-minute scans. 18+20 = 38, which matches the '38' in plan correction 1. (b) For the 20 reaction products the paper says the answer key came from one human expert who used a commercial database 'and suggestions from Dara', and success was counted as 'all peaks indexed', not 'right phases named'. So the only external-validity set in the plan has an answer key that is not independent of one graded tool. (c) The Dara authors state the tool fails when a phase is missing from the database and that lab powder XRD cannot settle composition. These three facts matter more to validity than the marking rule. They come from a small-model summary of the arXiv HTML page; re-read the exact wording before quoting it anywhere.

PRIOR-ART GAPS IN THE NOTES. plan.md and gaps.md contain no evaluation-methodology literature at all (no validity theory, Goodhart, leakage-in-science, materials-ML evaluation reviews). Direct overlaps the notes do not know: AFLOW-XtalFinder (N1), Alampara et al. 2025 and REFORMS and BetterBench (N5), NoiseEstimator (N4), Meredig LOCO-CV and formula-grouped Starrydata splits already in print (D3/N2), Miller 2024 and Card 2020 (D4). N2's premise 'TE papers split at random' is now partly false: at least one 2025 Starrydata paper groups by reduced formula. Since plan correction 17 says most of the jump comes from unseen formulas, the split already in use captures most of the effect. What is left for N2 is the smaller paper-level residual (24.8% to 29.4%) and the frozen DOI list.

DISCLOSURES. (1) Tool side effect: when I fetched the arXiv PDF of Manheim and Garrabrant to confirm the four Goodhart variants, the WebFetch tool saved the PDF binary to its own tool-results folder under ~/.claude/projects/.../4306e524-8308-4b33-8c27-c48b1baaf736/tool-results/. This conflicts with the no-PDF-to-disk rule. I did not delete it (read-only rule) and used only abstract or HTML pages afterwards. (2) opened=true means I fetched that URL in this run and a small summarising model reported the content; I did not read full texts. (3) Not opened, cited from memory or search snippets only and flagged opened=false: Messick 1995, Sambasivan 2021, Donoho 2017, Crusius 2025, Raven and Self 2017, the two 2026 ScienceDirect TE papers, pymatgen StructureMatcher docs. Publisher pages that demanded sign-in were not followed. (4) 'Criterion contamination' in P5 is a textbook psychometrics term used from memory, not a citation. (5) The AM Bench figure (3 submissions vs 6,044 downloads) is quoted from gaps.md G34, not re-verified. (6) Files read: <session-scratchpad>, .../synth/gaps.md, .../synth/storyline.md, .../synth/glossary_usermodel.md, .../synth/builds.md (grep), .../page/big-picture.html (section 'next'). Nothing was written, moved or deleted by me.

principles.name: Name the decision and the decider
principles.plain: A score is never valid in general. It is valid for one stated use. Before building an eval, write who will decide what from its number.
principles.how_to_check: For each planned eval item, can you fill in this line with a role outside this chat: 'ROLE will choose between A and B using this number'? Yes or no per item.
principles.why_it_matters_here: Only the user's own project passes today (0.309 vs 0.745, n=55), and that is an internal user. D4, N1, N4 and N5 have no named decider. plan.md section 8 admits 'who is we' is unconfirmed. Without a decider, nobody can say which marking tier or which interval width is 'right'.

sources.title: Validating the Interpretations and Uses of Test Scores (J. Educational Measurement 50(1))
sources.what_it_says: What gets validated is the proposed interpretation and use of a score, not the test. More ambitious claims need more support.

sources.title: The Heilmeier Catechism
sources.what_it_says: Eight questions for any project, including who cares, what difference success makes, and what the mid-term and final exams are.

principles.name: Exam task must stand for real skill
principles.plain: Construct validity: the test task must exercise the skill the real job needs. Naming known powders in a weighed mixture (ground truth by recipe) is not the same skill as analysing a real reaction product with shifted, disordered, poorly crystalline or unlisted phases.
principles.how_to_check: Is there measured evidence that tool rankings on weighed mixtures match tool rankings on real reaction products, for the same tools? If no, does every claim say 'on weighed mixtures' and nothing wider? Fail if neither.
principles.why_it_matters_here: Plan correction 2: the marking rule moves 1 to 3 of 20 on reaction products; the tool gap is 11 to 13 of 20. The Dara paper reports 20/20 on its 8-minute weighed scans but 15/20 on reaction products, and says the tool fails when a phase is not in the database. A 2024 critique found two thirds of one autonomous lab's claimed new materials were likely known disordered compounds (atoms sharing sites). Disorder is the real failure mode, and weighed mixtures of pure powders contain none. gaps.md also records one tool finding four different three-phase answers with near-identical fit: the measurement itself may not pin down the answer.

sources.title: Measurement and Fairness
sources.what_it_says: Unobservable constructs are measured through a model of how they show up in data; harm comes from mismatch between construct and measurement. Introduces construct validity and reliability for computational systems.

sources.title: AI and the Everything in the Whole Wide World Benchmark

principles.name: Cover the failure modes that matter
principles.plain: Content validity: list the real-world ways phase identification fails first. Then count test items per failure mode. Empty rows are named gaps, not silence.
principles.how_to_check: Does a written coverage table exist with rows such as: phase not in database; solid solution or shifted lattice; amorphous (non-crystalline) content; minor phase under about 5 wt%; preferred orientation; 4 or more phases; and a count of test items in each row? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: D1's roughly 25 tricky pairs cover naming ambiguity only (NiO vs Ni1.875O2, Nb2O5 vs Nb12O29). D6/N3 add more phases, still known powders. No planned item covers 'phase not in database', which is the tool authors' own stated limit. The Reynolds Cup (blind mineral contest) uses realistic clay-bearing mixtures, and its 12-year review names poorly crystalline clays as the main error source.

principles.name: External validity before internal polish
principles.plain: First show the result transfers to the real setting, a second test set, or a second instrument. Only then tighten marking rules, intervals and splits.
principles.how_to_check: Count planned desk-days by type. Are more days spent on internal validity (marking, ties, splits, noise) than on external validity (second measured set, second instrument or lab, real reaction products)? If yes, fail. Also: is every comparative claim backed by at least two independent test sets, or labelled 'one set, one instrument'?
principles.why_it_matters_here: D1, D4, N1, N4 and D3 are all internal. Only D6/N3 and L1/L2 touch external validity and they come later. The 40 scans come from one lab's instrument; L2 is designed as a one-instrument exam; plan correction 29 admits 'one lab is enough' is reasoning, not evidence. D6/N3 (three harder public measured sets) is the cheapest external check and deserves to move up.

sources.title: Are We Learning Yet? A Meta Review of Evaluation Failures Across Machine Learning (NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks)
sources.what_it_says: Splits evaluation failures into internal validity (baselines, test-set reuse) and external validity (does progress transfer beyond the benchmark).

sources.title: The Benchmark Lottery
sources.what_it_says: Relative ranking of methods changes a lot with the choice of benchmark tasks.

principles.name: Answer key independent of graded tools
principles.plain: If the ground truth was produced with help from a tool being graded, the score partly measures the tool agreeing with itself. Psychometrics calls this criterion contamination.
principles.how_to_check: For each test set: was the answer key made by someone who had not seen any graded tool's output? Yes or no. For any planned specialist review: does the specialist mark blind first, before seeing the AI-drafted verdicts?
principles.why_it_matters_here: Weighed mixtures pass (the key is the recipe). The 20 reaction products do not: the Dara paper says its human expert used 'suggestions from Dara', and success was 'all peaks indexed', not 'right phases'. That set is the plan's only external-validity evidence and it feeds the '11 to 13 of 20 tool gap'. L1 has the same risk: D1's key is 'AI-drafted, not yet reviewed', so a specialist shown it will anchor on it. gaps.md G19 already noted 'judgment vs judgment' for another tool but did not connect it to this set.

sources.title: Dara: Automated multiple-hypothesis phase identification and refinement from powder X-ray diffraction
sources.what_it_says: Reaction-product ground truth came from a human expert using a commercial database and Dara's suggestions; patterns were counted by whether all peaks were indexed.

sources.title: Validating the Interpretations and Uses of Test Scores
sources.what_it_says: Each inference from observed response to claimed meaning needs its own backing; the scoring inference (is the key right) is the first link.

principles.name: Scoring rule must match the decision
principles.plain: Pick the metric from the decision it feeds, not from what is easy to compute or from a classification scheme.
principles.how_to_check: Is each marking tier (strict formula, lenient formula, structure-level) tied in writing to a named downstream use, for example 'did the synthesis make the target compound' versus 'which structure family formed'? If tiers are justified only by a crystallography naming scheme, fail.
principles.why_it_matters_here: N1 takes its tier names from a 1990 classification. Nobody has said which tier a synthesis chemist or an autonomous lab actually needs. The Dara authors say lab XRD cannot settle composition, so a strict-formula tier may demand more than the measurement can give. Matbench Discovery is the materials precedent: a good regression error hid a high false-positive rate at the decision threshold. sacreBLEU shows the modest, real value of a standard scorer: it fixed reporting, not the construct.

sources.title: Matbench Discovery -- A framework to evaluate machine learning crystal stability predictions
sources.what_it_says: Regression metrics and task-relevant classification metrics are misaligned; accurate regressors can still give many false positives near the decision boundary. Argues for prospective benchmarks.

sources.title: A Call for Clarity in Reporting BLEU Scores
sources.what_it_says: The same metric varies by up to 1.8 points across configurations; a shared scorer (sacreBLEU) removes that spread.

principles.name: Effect must beat noise and tool gap
principles.plain: A marking or split effect justifies a tool only if it is larger than sampling noise and changes which tool wins, on the data that matters.
principles.how_to_check: On the target data (reaction products, not only the 40 weighed scans): does changing the marking rule flip any tool ranking, or move a score by more than the interval half-width? Yes or no. If no, stop N1.
principles.why_it_matters_here: By D4's own example, 38 vs 35 of 40 is a tie (interval 0.0 to 15.0 points). With n of 20 to 40 almost nothing is resolvable. On reaction products the rule moves 1 to 3 of 20 and rankings hold. On the 8-minute weighed scans the best tool is at 20/20, so there is no room for a rule to matter. Users choosing a tool care about ranking; ImageNet's re-test showed absolute scores can drop 11 to 14% while rankings hold.

principles.name: Ask what gaming the exam breaks
principles.plain: Goodhart's law and consequential validity: before publishing a score, write how a tool could raise it without getting better at the real job, and what that tool would then get worse at.
principles.how_to_check: Is there one written paragraph per eval that names the cheapest way to game it? If that way is easy (restrict the candidate list to the known chemical system; always pick the most common polymorph; always or never abstain), is there a guard or a narrower claim? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: Weighed-mixture exams reward closed candidate lists. gaps.md G21 to G23 already record that fit residual is hackable and that closed-list classifiers at about 93% fail on open multiphase patterns. D1 allows 'cannot tell' in the key; good, but the scorer must not let always-abstain win, which ties to the user's own calibrated-abstention project. For TE, published values are public, so adversarial gaming is free and any TE benchmark is a practice exam.

principles.plain: An eval with no user outside its author is a private unit test. Get one named outside role to say 'I would use this' before building past the test stage.
principles.how_to_check: Has one role outside this chat (a maintainer of the open phase-ID tool, one diffraction specialist, or one benchmark maintainer) been shown the 40-row result and replied? Yes or no. Today: no.

Adopted benchmarks come mostly from a few elite institutions, so a newcomer cannot assume uptake. The smallest path is one message with the 40-row table attached, to the tool's maintainers or to one specialist. It needs the user's yes and the user sends it. If nobody replies after a fair wait, that is a result: stop the marking-kit line.

principles.name: Do the fork-deciding step first
principles.plain: Order work by uncertainty removed per day. Run slow, decisive asks in parallel from day one. Give every item a written kill result.
principles.how_to_check: Is the step that decides the fork (will one diffraction specialist engage) scheduled before, or in parallel with, the desk builds that depend on it? Yes or no. Does every item have one sentence: 'if we see X, we stop'? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The plan calls the specialist question 'the one question only you can answer', then places it after about two weeks of desk work. Replies take weeks, so waiting costs calendar time. The 40-row test (1 to 2 days) is correctly first: it is a test, not a build, and its table is the natural thing to show a specialist. Add one cheap column to it: scan time, since the best tool's headroom is only in the 2-minute scans. glossary_usermodel.md notes only 3 of 188 past action items had a done test; kill results fix that.

principles.name: Hidden exam needs a standing referee
principles.plain: A real benchmark needs three things: sequestered test data, a referee who scores submissions, and enrolled competitors. Without all three, call it a practice exam and promise nothing more.
principles.how_to_check: Does the plan name who will hold the hidden answers, score entries, and keep doing so for years? If no, is every output labelled 'practice exam' or 'one-off blind check'? Fail if neither.
principles.why_it_matters_here: L2 needs roughly 385 powders for plus or minus 5 points (470 to 780 if paired), one partner lab and a long-lived referee. The plan itself says this 'may be out of our reach'. Under this lens that is the dominant bottleneck, and it may indeed be out of reach for a small outside team. The Reynolds Cup shows what it takes: a society, a volunteer organiser each round, about 100 sample sets, 20+ years. The honest reachable version is a one-off blind check with one lab. TE values are public, so TE can never be hidden.

materials-ml-evals.lens: Evaluation work that already exists inside materials ML and autonomous labs: Matbench and Matbench Discovery, leave-one-cluster-out validation, MatFold, redundancy/leakage papers (MD-HIT), how thermoelectric (TE) ML papers split Starrydata, how automated powder-XRD phase identification is scored (Dara, XRD-AutoAnalyzer, opXRD, RADAR-PD, XRDBench, GALAXI, Reynolds Cup), and the Leeman 2024 dispute plus the 2026 author correction.

principles.name: Split by the unit that leaks
principles.plain: Rows that share a hidden cause must sit on the same side of the split. In TE data the hidden causes are the paper (same lab, same sample batch), the formula (one compound measured at many temperatures) and the chemical family. Always print a nearest-neighbour baseline beside the model.
principles.how_to_check: Does the results table show random, by-formula, by-paper and by-chemical-system scores side by side, each with a 1-nearest-neighbour row? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: D3 already does this (25.5 / 42.2 / 46.6 percent error; 1-NN at 21.4 percent). That part is on-principle. But grouping by formula is NOT new in TE: a 2026 ACS Omega paper uses GroupKFold by composition on Starrydata, and Na and Chang 2022 test on unseen material groups. What I did not find anywhere: grouping by paper (DOI). So the claim must shrink from 'TE papers split at random' to 'nobody groups by paper'. Plan correction 21 still stands: name the papers. Parse 2024 is a candidate but I could not confirm its split.

principles.name: Add a split by publication year
principles.plain: A forward-in-time split is the closest thing to real use. Train on what was known at a date. Test on what was published later.
principles.how_to_check: Does D3 include one split where every test paper is published after every training paper? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The plan has random, by-paper and by-chemical-system splits. A search of plan.md and gaps.md finds no time split. Starrydata rows carry a DOI, so the year is cheap to get. A year split also gives a test list that grows on its own, which is the natural base for L5. Caveat: later papers re-measure old compounds, so report it together with the seen/unseen-formula flag.

principles.name: Do not call grouped splits out-of-distribution
principles.plain: Holding out a group does not prove the test rows are far from training. Most 'out-of-distribution' splits in materials turn out to be interpolation. Measure the overlap and print it.
principles.how_to_check: For each held-out split, is there a number for how many test rows still have a near twin in training (same formula, same paper, or a stated distance cut-off)? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The plan already found this about itself: holding out by chemical system still leaves the test paper in training 52.4 percent of the time, and most of the 25.5-to-42.2 jump is unseen formulas. That is exactly the check. Keep those numbers in the headline table. Do not use the words 'extrapolation' or 'OOD' in N2.

principles.name: Freeze, clean and fence the test list
principles.plain: Publish three things: the exact test list, the rule that removes test items duplicating training items (with counts), and the rule for what training data is allowed. Without all three, two people's scores cannot be compared.
principles.how_to_check: Is there (a) a versioned file of test IDs, (b) a written de-duplication rule with the number removed, (c) a one-line allowed-training-data rule? Yes or no on each.
principles.why_it_matters_here: D3's frozen DOI list gives (a). For (b): D2 found 499 files identical across two XRD archives, so any XRD split that spans RRUFF and opXRD leaks unless de-duplicated first. For (c): ESTM is a subset of Starrydata, so a model pre-trained on ESTM is not a clean entrant on a Starrydata test list. Matbench Discovery removed about 11,000 test structures that matched training prototypes and still had a later leak through a third dataset.

sources.title: Matbench Discovery (full text, v3)
sources.what_it_says: Test set cut from 257,487 to 215,488 after removing structures matching a training prototype, pathological entries and duplicates. Models count as compliant only if trained on the named training snapshot or earlier.

principles.name: Pick the metric that matches the decision
principles.plain: Low average error does not mean good decisions. Report the number that matches the use: false-positive rate for screening, sign and size for a signed quantity, hit rate for discovery.
principles.how_to_check: Does each headline number come with one sentence naming the decision it supports, and is at least one decision-level metric reported (false-positive rate, sign accuracy, top-k hit rate)? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: Seebeck coefficient is signed (negative for electron carriers, positive for hole carriers) and passes through zero, so percent error blows up there. The plan already adds absolute error and sign accuracy. Good. For XRD the decision is 'did the synthesis make the target', so a spurious phase must cost as much as a missed one.

sources.title: Matbench Discovery
sources.what_it_says: Accurate regressors can still give many false positives near the stable/unstable boundary. Ranks models by classification metrics, not regression error.

sources.who: Borg, Muckley, Saal, Meredig and co-authors
sources.title: Quantifying the performance of machine learning models in materials discovery
sources.what_it_says: RMSE has no clear link to discovery success. Proposes Discovery Yield and Discovery Probability.

principles.name: Reproduce the published marks before re-marking
principles.plain: Before proposing a new marking rule, reproduce the original authors' marks pattern by pattern under their own rule. Otherwise the gap may come from your harness, not from the field.
principles.how_to_check: Is there a table lining up the Dara paper's per-pattern verdicts (its published benchmark spreadsheets) against the local run, with every mismatch tagged as library, settings or marking? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The Dara paper states its rule: a pattern is right only if every weighed-in ingredient is found and no spurious phase is reported. It is marked per pattern, and summaries are published as two spreadsheets. The plan's 12 / 17 / 32 of 40 spread comes from the user's own formula-string marker plus a different reference library (open COD capped at 80 candidates, versus licensed ICSD in the paper). A reviewer will call the marking-rule finding a harness artefact until D1 lines up with that spreadsheet. Move N1's 'does Dara ship its own marking script' check into week 1. I saw no scoring script on the repository landing page. That is not proof of absence.

sources.title: Dara: Automated multiple-hypothesis phase identification and refinement from powder X-ray diffraction

sources.title: idocx/dara (MIT licence)

principles.name: Score phases, not only whole patterns
principles.plain: Per-pattern exact match hides whether errors are misses or false alarms. Also report per-phase precision, recall and F1. When the recipe weights are known, report weight error too.
principles.how_to_check: Does the marker output per-phase true positives, false positives and false negatives (micro-F1) beside the per-pattern score, and a weight-error score for weighed mixtures? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: These are the rulers the community already uses. GALAXI (Sept 2026) reports micro-F1 0.935 on curated measured patterns. The Reynolds Cup (a mineral-analysis contest with known mixtures) ranks entrants by summed deviation from true weight percent. The 2001 crystallography-union round robin used a Kullback-Leibler-type distance. A search of gaps.md finds no per-phase precision or recall. If N1 prints these, its numbers can sit beside published ones.

principles.name: Make the same-phase rule deterministic and versioned
principles.plain: Whether two database entries count as 'the same phase' must be a written rule that a script applies identically every time. An LLM judge or a human eye is not reproducible.
principles.how_to_check: Can a stranger re-run the marker on the same results file and get identical marks, and is there a test file of tricky pairs with expected verdicts? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: RADAR-PD decides equivalence with a second GPT-4 prompt built to tolerate supercells, hydration differences and lower-symmetry variants. That proves the problem is real and unsolved. Leeman's core complaint is ordered versus disordered versions of one compound (atoms on fixed sites versus randomly mixed sites). D1's 25-pair CSV plus N1's tiers is this gap. I found nobody shipping a deterministic rule. This item is open and well aimed. The risk is that tier boundaries are a materials judgement, hence L1.

principles.name: The answer key must stand without the tool
principles.plain: Ground truth should come from something independent of the method under test: a weighed recipe, a second measurement technique, or specialist agreement. A key drafted by a fitting tool or an LLM inherits their blind spots.
principles.how_to_check: Does every benchmark row record its truth source as one of {weighed recipe, independent measurement, specialist-agreed, tool- or AI-drafted}, and are tool- or AI-drafted rows kept out of headline numbers? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: Weighed mixtures (Dara's 40, Reynolds Cup, the crystallography-union sets) pass. RADAR-PD's labels were built by GPT-4 selection plus a fit-quality filter, so they do not. The A-Lab correction conceded that 4 of 40 identifications cannot be settled by diffraction alone, so an XRD-only key has a ceiling. For the plan: the tricky-pairs CSV is AI-drafted until L1 happens. Fine for private use. Do not publish it as a key before a specialist signs.

principles.name: State the candidate library and its coverage
principles.plain: A phase-ID tool can only name phases that are in its reference library. Scores from different libraries are not comparable. Say which library, which version, how candidates were shortlisted, and whether the true phases were in the pool.
principles.how_to_check: Does every score row carry library name and version, the candidate-pool rule, and a per-scan flag 'all true phases were in the pool'? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: Dara's paper used ICSD (licensed). The local run uses COD (open) capped at 80 candidates. GALAXI trains on COD. RADAR-PD ran both tools over a combined COD plus Materials Project pool and does not say whether that is Dara's native set-up. Much of the 38-versus-32 of 40 gap is this. N3 already has the flag. D1 needs it too, or the week-1 result is confounded.

principles.name: Count independent units and show intervals
principles.plain: n is the number of independent things, not the number of rows. Compare two tools on the same items with a paired method. Put an interval on every score.
principles.how_to_check: Does D4 resample by cluster (mixture for XRD, paper for TE) and use a paired comparison when both tools ran on the same scans? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: Dara's 40 scans are 20 mixtures at two scan times, so about 20 independent units. principles.name: Test on measured data; label simulated data
principles.plain: Models trained on computed patterns lose accuracy on measured ones. A benchmark must say, per file, measured or computed, and report the two apart.

principles.name: Report the noise ceiling
principles.plain: Labels carry measurement error. No model can beat the disagreement between repeat measurements. Print that floor beside the model error so nobody chases noise.
principles.how_to_check: Is there a label-noise number (repeat-measurement or across-paper spread) beside each model error, and is every claimed gain larger than it? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The plan already has this for TE: a lookup allowed to see the answers still misses by 15.0 percent, and one formula differs across papers by a median 32.7 percent. That is the strongest part of the TE story. Crusius and co-authors did the same for nine chemistry and materials datasets and ship a tool. N4 (noise ladder) overlaps it: cite it and check whether it can be reused before building. I could not open it (403).

principles.name: Say what the score claims to measure
principles.plain: Write down the real-world ability the benchmark stands for and why the task is a fair proxy. Ship that as a short card with the benchmark.
principles.how_to_check: Is there a one-page card per benchmark with: the claimed ability, data source, known label problems, split rule, metric, and what a high score does NOT mean? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The likeliest reviewer attack on the TE work: predicting Seebeck from the formula alone is a weak construct. Doping level and sample processing drive the value, and the formula string hides them. N2 already asks a TE specialist to sign off the task definition. Keep that as a gate, not a nicety.
