materials-ml-evals.notes:
VERDICT FOR THIS LENS. Yes, this is evaluation work, and most of it is aimed right. Against the 14 checks, the plan already passes or nearly passes P1 (grouped splits plus 1-NN), P3 (overlap measured), P5 (sign and absolute error), P12 (D2), P13 (noise floor). It fails or is silent on P2 (no time split), P6 (own marks not yet lined up with the paper's spreadsheet), P7 (no per-phase precision/recall or weight error), P11 (D4 is unpaired and unclustered), P14 (no card; N5 overlaps existing work). P4, P8, P9, P10 are partly met and cheap to finish.

WHERE A MATERIALS-ML REVIEWER WOULD SAY IT IS MIS-AIMED.
1. Field-wide claims from 40 scans (about 20 independent mixtures, one lab, one chemistry space). The plan admits this; keep the claim local.
2. The 12 / 17 / 32 of 40 spread may be an artefact of the user's own formula-string marker and a different library. The community marks by reference entry or by eye. D1 is the right test. Do not state the finding before D1 lines up with Dara's spreadsheet.
3. 'TE papers split at random' is partly wrong. Formula-grouped validation already exists (one paper opened, one seen in a snippet, plus an unseen-group test from 2022). The open part is grouping by paper, a year split, a frozen list and the noise floor. Katsura 2022 must be read first; I could not open it.
4. Seebeck-from-formula is a weak construct because doping and processing drive the value. Keep the specialist sign-off in N2 as a gate.
5. Hidden exams are not new in this field. Reynolds Cup and the JARVIS experimental track are working models. Cite and copy their logistics for L2 and L5.
6. N4 overlaps NoiseEstimator. N5 overlaps evaluation cards and model info sheets. Both should shrink to 'cite and apply'.
OPEN AND WORTH DOING: a deterministic same-phase rule with a test file (P8); by-paper and by-year TE splits with a frozen list; the measured/computed audit (D2).

HONESTY NOTES. Could not open (403, 406 or sign-in redirect): Crusius 2025, Madsen 2001, Parse 2024, the SHAP TE paper, Katsura 2022, Omee 2024, OMat24 full text, the C&EN news piece. Each is marked opened=false. Miller 2024 is from memory and outside the lens. GALAXI, AutoXRD, MD-HIT, Borg, Li 2023, Li 2025, Kapoor, Alampara, JARVIS, opXRD, teMatDb, Szymanski 2021: abstract pages only. MatFold and Na and Chang: README only. Meredig: the Citrine summary page, not the journal page. Matbench (Dunn 2020) was opened at abstract level but is not cited above because the nested-CV detail I wanted was not on the page. 'No scoring script in the Dara repo' and 'no by-paper TE audit' are negative searches, not proof of absence. gaps.md ends at a NEXT7 marker, so Theme 7 (G42 to G50) was not available to me. already_in_notes means plan.md or gaps.md; where another notes file knows the item I say so.

SECURITY NOTE. One fetched web page returned text styled as a system reminder about git commit attribution. It came from a tool result, not from the user. I ignored it; no commits were made and no files were written.

Files read (read-only): <session-scratchpad> and .../scratchpad/synth/gaps.md; builds.md, glossary_usermodel.md, storyline.md and plan/verify_K2_prior-art.md were searched by keyword only.

measurement-science.lens: How analytical chemistry, crystallography and metrology already test a measurement or analysis method: round robins, proficiency testing and its scoring (ISO 13528, ISO/IEC 17043, IUPAC protocol), certified reference materials, blind weighed-mixture contests (Reynolds Cup, IUCr CPD QPA round robin, the 2002 search-match round robin), detection limits, and the physical reasons a weighed mixture is not a perfect answer key.

principles.name: Say exactly what is being measured
principles.plain: A test is only valid for a stated task and range. Naming the phases (identification) and giving their amounts (quantification) are different tasks, and the old contests kept them apart on purpose.
principles.how_to_check: Does the eval card state, one line each: task (name phases only, or name plus amounts), naming level required, wt% range covered, sample type (weighed mixture or real product), and instrument or radiation? If any line is blank, fail.
principles.why_it_matters_here: D6 and N3 plan to re-use scans from the IUCr quantification round robin as a phase-naming practice exam. In the original test the organisers told every entrant which phases were present. Re-using the scans for naming is fine, but it is a new use that the original key was never validated for. Say so on the card. The Reynolds Cup gives no phase list, so it is the closer precedent for a naming exam.

sources.title: Quantitative Phase Analysis Round Robin: letter to participants
sources.what_it_says: Phase identities and full structure data were supplied to every entrant because the aim was to test quantification, not identification. Goals listed include accuracy, precision and lower limits of detection.

sources.title: The Reynolds Cup (rules and guidelines page)
sources.what_it_says: Rule 1: no qualitative information is given, so entrants must both identify and quantify. Rule 2: any method is allowed.

sources.title: The Fitness for Purpose of Analytical Methods: a laboratory guide to method validation, 2nd ed.
sources.what_it_says: From memory, not opened in this run: validation starts from a stated measurand, scope and working range; results outside the scope are not covered.

principles.name: The answer key needs its own check
principles.plain: A weighed recipe is a claim, not the truth. Each ingredient must be checked for purity, and the mixed recipe must be confirmed by an independent measurement, with an error bar on every weight fraction.
principles.how_to_check: For every mixture, is there (a) a scan of each pure ingredient showing no second phase above a stated limit, (b) one independent check of the mix (bulk chemistry such as XRF, or a second analysis method), and (c) a stated uncertainty on each wt%? Three yes answers, or fail.
principles.why_it_matters_here: L2 (hidden exam with a partner lab, about 385 powders) says nothing about ingredient purity. If a bought chemical holds 3% of a second phase, that phase is really in the scan and a correct tool gets marked as a false positive. Even the NIST purity standard is only about 99% crystalline, because every grain has a thin non-crystalline skin. So weighed fraction and crystalline fraction differ by up to a few percent in fine powders. The notes already found hydrated chemicals stored under dry formulas in the user's own data, which is the same failure.

sources.title: Outcomes of the IUCr CPD Round Robin on Quantitative Phase Analysis: samples 1a to 1h (J. Appl. Cryst. 34, 409-426)
sources.what_it_says: Weighed values were cross-checked by XRF on three randomly chosen portions plus three in-house analysis methods. Spread was typically under about 0.5% relative, rising to 3-4% relative at the 1 wt% level.

sources.title: The Reynolds Cup (rules and guidelines page)
sources.what_it_says: Organiser guidelines: purity of the minerals used is known within 1 wt%; a repeatable splitting procedure is used; splits are verified by XRD and XRF before shipping.

sources.who: Cline, Von Dreele, Winburn, Stephens, Filliben (NIST)
sources.title: Addressing the amorphous content issue in quantitative phase analysis: the certification of NIST SRM 676a
sources.what_it_says: The certified alumina standard has a phase purity of 99.02% +/- 1.11%. A non-diffracting surface layer exists on any crystal and can be several percent of the mass in a fine powder.

principles.name: No ranking inside the key's error
principles.plain: If two entrants differ by less than the uncertainty of the answer key (plus sampling error), call it a tie. Proficiency-test statistics widen the score when the key itself is uncertain.
principles.how_to_check: Does the tie function take two inputs, sampling error from the number of items AND a stated key error rate? Does any 'A beats B' sentence in the write-up survive both? If the key error is not stated, fail.
principles.why_it_matters_here: D4 (38/40 vs 35/40 returns tie) handles sampling error only. The 25-row tricky-pairs key is AI-drafted and unchecked until L1, so its own error rate is unknown and probably larger than the gap between tools. The Reynolds Cup does the same thing by rule: entries inside the mixtures' uncertainty are not separated on the main score. This supports D4 and tells you to add the second input.

sources.title: The Reynolds Cup (rules and guidelines page)
sources.what_it_says: Rule 6: winner is the smallest sum of absolute errors; if several entries fall within the established uncertainties of the mixture compositions, stricter tie-break criteria are applied (clay bias, relative errors, count of missed or misidentified phases).

sources.title: ISO 13528:2022 Statistical methods for use in proficiency testing by interlaboratory comparison
sources.what_it_says: From memory, not opened (ISO site blocked the fetcher; URL from memory): the uncertainty of the assigned value should be below about 0.3 of the scoring standard deviation; otherwise use the z-prime score, which adds the key's uncertainty to the denominator.

sources.title: The International Harmonized Protocol for the proficiency testing of analytical chemistry laboratories (Pure Appl. Chem. 78, 145-196)
sources.what_it_says: Search result and memory only (publisher page showed a bot wall): the scoring spread should be set by fitness for purpose, not by the spread of the entrants, and the assigned value's uncertainty must be reported.

principles.name: Prove the test items are uniform and stable
principles.plain: Before items are used, show that splits of the same powder agree with each other and that the powder does not change between mixing and scanning.
principles.how_to_check: Is there a written homogeneity check (re-scan or re-split a random subset, compare against a preset limit) and a stability rule (date mixed, date scanned, air-sensitive or water-absorbing ingredients flagged)? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: L2 asks a partner lab to hand-mix hundreds of small powders. Two physical problems hit small samples. First, a 1 wt% ingredient in a few hundred milligrams may be only a handful of grains in the beam, so its peaks are a lottery (particle statistics). Second, many oxide, hydroxide and carbonate ingredients take up water or CO2 from air, so the recipe drifts. The standard criterion is simple: between-sample spread at most 0.3 of the scoring tolerance.

sources.who: Shapypro (secondary explainer of ISO 13528 Annex B)
sources.title: ISO 13528 homogeneity and stability
sources.what_it_says: Homogeneity passes if between-sample SD is at most 0.3 of the scoring SD; stability passes if the before/after difference is at most 0.3 of the scoring SD. If it fails, fold the extra spread into the score or use z-prime. Secondary source; the ISO text itself was not opened.

sources.title: The Reynolds Cup (rules and guidelines page)
sources.what_it_says: About 100 sample sets per round are produced with a repeatable splitting procedure and the splits are verified for consistency by XRD and XRF before distribution.

sources.title: Outcomes of the IUCr CPD Round Robin on QPA: samples 1a to 1h
sources.what_it_says: Three randomly selected portions of each mixture were analysed to confirm the weighed values before results were judged.

principles.name: Separate reading a scan from making one
principles.plain: Test the analysis step on fixed, supplied scans, and test sample preparation plus measurement separately. One instrument gives repeatability only; it says nothing about other instruments.
principles.how_to_check: Does every headline number carry the label 'fixed scans, one instrument'? Is there a named, sized second-instrument subset planned before any claim that a tool 'works on lab XRD'? If the claim is general and the data is one instrument, fail.
principles.why_it_matters_here: An ML phase-naming tool only does the analysis half, so the right old analogue is the round robin's supplied-data arm, not the whole contest. The plan already calls L2 a one-instrument exam, which is correct. Correction 29 (one lab is enough is reasoning, not a measured fact) is exactly the repeatability versus reproducibility distinction. The round robin showed the two arms give different scores on the same sample.

sources.title: Quantitative Phase Analysis Round Robin: letter to participants
sources.what_it_says: Three levels of participation: analyse CPD-supplied scans only; measure supplied prepared samples; prepare and measure unprepared samples. Instrument settings were left to each participant.

sources.who: Scarlett, Madsen, Cranswick, Lwin, Groleau, Stephenson, Aylmore, Agron-Olshina
sources.title: Outcomes of the IUCr CPD Round Robin on QPA: samples 2, 3, 4, synthetic bauxite, natural granodiorite and pharmaceuticals (J. Appl. Cryst. 35, 383-400)
sources.what_it_says: For the microabsorption sample, the error score with supplied scans differed clearly from the score with participants' own scans, and from neutron data. So the measurement step and the analysis step contribute separately.

sources.title: The Fitness for Purpose of Analytical Methods, 2nd ed.
sources.what_it_says: From memory, not opened: repeatability (same lab, same kit, short time) and reproducibility (different labs) are distinct precision measures and must not be swapped.

principles.name: Put known physical traps in on purpose
principles.plain: The field knows which physical effects break powder XRD. A credible test includes items built to trigger each one, labels them, and reports results per label.
principles.how_to_check: Does each item carry tags for: strong absorption contrast between ingredients, plate- or needle-shaped ingredient, non-crystalline ingredient, poorly crystalline ingredient, grain size known? Is there at least one item per tag, and a per-tag score? If the only difficulty axis is counting noise, fail.
principles.why_it_matters_here: N4 (noise ladder) varies random noise only. A diffraction person will say random noise is the smallest problem. The real ones are systematic: microabsorption (grains of a heavy phase shade themselves, so their peaks come out weak), preferred orientation (flat or needle grains lie down, so some peaks are too strong), non-crystalline content (no sharp peaks at all), and peak overlap. The 1998 round robin built one sample per effect. G20 already notes summed scans are about 5 points off from absorption; this principle turns that note into a design rule.

sources.title: Quantitative Phase Analysis Round Robin: letter to participants
sources.what_it_says: Sample 1 is the easy baseline. Sample 2 adds a platy phase (preferred orientation). Sample 3 adds silica glass (non-crystalline content). Sample 4 mixes phases of very different absorption with known grain sizes (microabsorption). A 7-phase synthetic bauxite, a natural rock and two drug mixtures follow.

sources.title: Outcomes of the IUCr CPD Round Robin on QPA: samples 2, 3, 4, synthetic bauxite, natural granodiorite and pharmaceuticals
sources.what_it_says: The two main obstacles were microabsorption, which may be insurmountable with X-rays for some material suites, and operator error. The standard absorption correction helped in some cases and was over-applied in others.

sources.title: The effect of grain or particle size on X-ray reflections from mixed powders and alloys (Phil. Mag. 36, 347-369)
sources.what_it_says: From memory, not opened (DOI from memory): the classic microabsorption model; the correction depends on grain size and absorption contrast, both of which must be known.

principles.name: Report detection by amount, with a floor
principles.plain: Give the hit rate as a curve against how much of the phase is present, in bands fixed in advance. Mark the band below the instrument's physical floor as 'not expected to be visible', not as a tool failure.
principles.how_to_check: Are wt% bands fixed before running, does each band show item count and an interval, and is there a declared floor (with its source) below which misses are not counted against the tool? Three yes answers, or fail.
principles.why_it_matters_here: N3 already fixes bands in advance, which is right. What it lacks is the floor. A very careful lab study put the detection limit near 0.2 wt% for a well-crystallised phase on a copper-source instrument, with useful accuracy only above 1 wt%. Fast routine scans are worse. That same public set (León-Reina, 0.12 to 4.0 wt%) sits largely near the floor, so a low score there says little about the tool. G28 in the notes already says 'not found' needs a bound; this gives the number.

sources.who: León-Reina, García-Maté, Álvarez-Pinazo, Santacruz, Vallcorba, De la Torre, Aranda
sources.title: Accuracy in Rietveld quantitative phase analysis: a comparative study of strictly monochromatic Mo and Cu radiations (J. Appl. Cryst. 49)
sources.what_it_says: Abstract: 78 analyses. Detection limit about 0.2 wt% (Cu) and 0.3 wt% (Mo). Quantification limit near 0.10 wt% but with relative error near 100%. Only above 1.0 wt% was relative error under 20%.

sources.title: Outcomes of the IUCr CPD Round Robin on QPA: samples 1a to 1h
sources.what_it_says: A 10% relative error at 1 wt% is not the same as at 90 wt%, so the organisers used a concentration-weighted Kullback-Leibler distance as the single error score rather than averaging relative errors.

principles.name: Wrong extra phases cost as much as misses
principles.plain: Automated search tools over-report. The contest community found that naming phases that are not there is the largest single error source, so the score must punish it directly.
principles.how_to_check: Does the score sheet show a separate false-positive count per scan (not only recall or a blended F1)? Does the exam include single-phase items and items where the right answer is a short list? If precision is not reported on its own, fail.
principles.why_it_matters_here: N3 and L2 score lists of named phases. Fit-driven tools can always lower the misfit by adding another phase (G23 already flags the fit residual as a hackable reward). The contest page calls misidentified phases "THE biggest source of bias". A 2019 automatic tool had to cap its list because it kept adding plausible phases near 1%. Trap items with one phase are the cheapest defence.

sources.title: The Reynolds Cup (rules and guidelines page)
sources.what_it_says: Advice to entrants: do not rely solely on automated search/match; misidentifying absent phases is the biggest bias source; cross-check against bulk chemistry. Tie-breaks count non-identified and misidentified phases.

sources.title: Outcomes of 12 years of the Reynolds Cup quantitative mineral analysis round robin (Clays and Clay Minerals 65, 122-134)
sources.what_it_says: Abstract: 448 participants, about 14,000 analyses, 21 samples. Top entrants found all or most phases. Poor entries missed or misnamed phases; long lists of exotic minor phases likely came from automated search-match and were implausible.

sources.title: Full-profile search-match by the Rietveld method (J. Appl. Cryst. 52, 587-598)
sources.what_it_says: A plain fit-quality index was not good enough to rank candidate phases, so penalties were added. Without a cap the tool adds several extra phases near 1% that cannot be checked.

principles.name: Publish naming levels before the test
principles.plain: Decide in advance which answers count as the same (same family, same series, same structure type), with a number for every tolerance. Also list what a powder scan cannot distinguish at all.
principles.how_to_check: Is there a grouping table, frozen before any scoring, with a numeric tolerance per tier, plus a list of pair types declared unanswerable from a lab powder scan? If grading choices are made after seeing answers, fail.
principles.why_it_matters_here: This is D1 and N1. The plan's 'cannot tell' verdict and guard rows are the right instinct and have precedent: the Reynolds Cup ships a spreadsheet of minimum naming levels, and the 2002 search-match round robin accepted a neighbouring series member as correct. Two things a specialist would add. First, the 1990 tier names come with no tolerances; the report itself notes the verdict flips depending on where the similarity limit is set. ICSD structure types are a worked, rule-based version. Second, 'cannot tell' depends on scan quality, not only on the pair: mirror-image pairs are always identical in powder data, but ordered versus disordered differs by weak extra peaks that only a long scan shows.

sources.title: The Reynolds Cup (rules and guidelines page)
sources.what_it_says: Rule 5: minerals are grouped for judging, and a spreadsheet given to entrants states the minimum categorisation level required.

sources.title: Search-Match Round Robin 2002: results page (paper: Powder Diffraction 18, 106-113, 2003)
sources.what_it_says: Four real samples. Grading was lenient and human-judged: a member of the same mineral series, or a magnesium-bearing carbonate in place of the iron one, was accepted. Only one entrant found all ten phases.

sources.who: Lima-de-Faria, Hellner, Liebau, Makovicky, Parthé (IUCr nomenclature report)
sources.title: Nomenclature of inorganic structure types (Acta Cryst. A46, 1-11)
sources.what_it_says: Defines four similarity tiers (isopointal, isoconfigurational, crystal-chemically isotypic, homeotypic). Mirror-image space-group pairs count as the same type. A footnote notes that whether two structures with axis ratios 30% apart are the same type depends on the chosen limit.

sources.title: The introduction of structure types into the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database ICSD (Acta Cryst. A63, 412-417)
sources.what_it_says: Abstract: structure types are assigned by stepwise rules: space group, Wyckoff sequence, Pearson symbol, then axis-ratio and angle ranges, formula type, and required or forbidden elements.

principles.name: Fix and log what the entrant was given
principles.plain: Results depend heavily on the reference database version and on hints such as which elements are present. Record both for every run and never pool results across them.
principles.how_to_check: Does each result row record: reference database name and date, whether the element list was given, and whether every true phase was in the candidate list? Are scores reported separately for each setting? If any of the three is missing, fail.
principles.why_it_matters_here: N3's 'truth in candidate list' flag is exactly this and should stay. Add the hint level. In the 2002 round robin about 16% of entrants failed one sample only because their database was too old, and one phase was missing from the database entirely. In 2019 an automatic tool could not finish the same sample because the structure was not in the open database. In real synthesis work the elements are always known, so an exam without them tests a harder and less relevant task. Pick one and state it.

sources.title: Search-Match Round Robin 2002: results page
sources.what_it_says: Two steps: scans with a vague origin, then scans plus chemistry. About 16% could not identify one sample because their database release was too old. One polymorph was absent from the database. Conclusion: software, expert hands and a current database are all needed.

sources.title: Full-profile search-match by the Rietveld method
sources.what_it_says: Result quality depends mainly on whether the sought phase is in the structure database. One round-robin sample could not be completed for that reason. Runs were reported both with and without element restrictions.

sources.title: Quantitative Phase Analysis Round Robin: letter to participants
sources.what_it_says: Entrants were given the phase list and crystal-structure data, and the letter states this explicitly as part of the test definition.

principles.name: Freeze settings; the operator is a variable
principles.plain: Round robins found that who runs the software, and with what settings, moves the result more than which method is used. A tool's score is really the score of tool plus settings plus operator.
principles.how_to_check: Is each tool run from a frozen, published configuration with no per-scan human adjustment, and is the configuration recorded with the score? Is it flagged when the tool's authors could have tuned on the same public scans? If a human touched individual scans, fail.
principles.why_it_matters_here: N3 runs Dara on public sets and reports whether they are still too easy. That sentence is only true for one configuration. Public round-robin scans have been used as development examples by tool authors (the 2019 paper did), so a good score may be partly memorised. The old finding cuts both ways: on the easy sample, a locked-down automatic run beat the average human entrant, because the restrictions prevented operator mistakes.

sources.title: Outcomes of the IUCr CPD Round Robin on QPA: samples 1a to 1h
sources.what_it_says: Even on a sample designed to avoid physical problems, and even on identical supplied scans, results varied widely. Causes: wrong reference ratios, software misuse, poor crystallographic understanding, over-correction. Many gave no error estimate.

sources.title: Outcomes of the IUCr CPD Round Robin on QPA: samples 2, 3, 4, synthetic bauxite, natural granodiorite and pharmaceuticals
sources.what_it_says: Recommends standard strategies and checklists, but warns against reducing the analysis to a black box.

sources.title: Full-profile search-match by the Rietveld method
sources.what_it_says: A fully automatic, heavily restricted run on round-robin sample 1h landed within 2% absolute of the weighed values, tighter than the spread of the human entrants. The authors credit the restrictions.

principles.name: Reproduce a certified answer before building anything
principles.plain: Run the whole pipeline first on an item whose answer was certified or contest-verified by someone else. If it cannot reproduce that answer, nothing built on top can be trusted.
principles.how_to_check: Has the marker-plus-tool pipeline been run on at least one externally verified item (for example the round robin's supplied scans of the three-phase sample, or a scan of a certified reference mixture) and returned the known phases? Yes or no.
principles.why_it_matters_here: This is a cheap positive control the plan lacks, and it fits D6 (web-only check of public weighed sets). The round robin's supplied scans are small text files with weighed values public since 1999; the 2019 paper used them as its first test. In cement, a lab must qualify against NIST reference clinkers under ASTM C1365, within per-phase limits, before its numbers count. Any download still needs the user's yes.

sources.title: Cement characteristics: direct phase assessment (programme page)
sources.what_it_says: ASTM C1365 is the standardised XRD method for cement and clinker phases. Reference clinkers SRM 2686, 2687, 2688 and 2686a were certified using XRD and microscopy.

sources.who: Instrument vendor application note hosted by AZoM
sources.title: Clinker phase analysis checked against ASTM C1365 limits
sources.what_it_says: 21 repeat analyses of the NIST clinkers compared with C1365 per-phase precision limits (about 0.2 to 0.7 wt% at one sigma, depending on phase). Vendor source; used only to show how qualification works.

sources.title: Full-profile search-match by the Rietveld method
sources.what_it_says: First test of the new tool was round-robin data set 1h from the IUCr CPD site, compared against the weighed values and the entrants' spread.

sources.who: Cline, Von Dreele, Winburn, Stephens, Filliben (NIST)
sources.title: Certification of NIST SRM 676a
sources.what_it_says: A certified alumina powder exists specifically to anchor quantitative powder diffraction, with a stated purity and uncertainty.

principles.name: Weighed mixtures are the easy case
principles.plain: Real reaction products contain mixed-composition phases, unknown phases and poorly crystalline material that no weighed mixture has. Accuracy on weighed mixtures is an upper bound, and keys for real samples need an appeal path.
principles.how_to_check: Does the write-up call weighed-mixture accuracy an upper bound in plain words? Is there a planned second arm on real products, scored against expert consensus, with a written way to challenge and revise the key? If the weighed exam is presented as 'real-world accuracy', fail.
principles.why_it_matters_here: The long-term aim (L2) is weighed mixtures only. The round robin's natural rock had no known answer at all. The 2002 search-match samples were real, with admittedly inexact solutions. In 2019 an automatic tool disagreed with the organisers' key on one phase, and a manual refinement put that phase near zero. So published keys can be wrong and were revised by later work. G19 (no multi-rater truth) already points here; this adds the appeal rule.

sources.title: Outcomes of the IUCr CPD Round Robin on QPA: samples 2, 3, 4, synthetic bauxite, natural granodiorite and pharmaceuticals
sources.what_it_says: For the natural rock the correct answer is unknown: minor phases may be present that diffraction does not easily detect, and each phase's real composition may differ from its nominal formula.

sources.title: Search-Match Round Robin 2002: results page
sources.what_it_says: Samples were real-life materials, not weighed mixtures, and the organisers state the database does not always hold exact solutions.

sources.title: Full-profile search-match by the Rietveld method
sources.what_it_says: On one round-robin sample the tool did not find a phase the organisers listed; a manual refinement with that phase forced in gave an amount close to zero. It also found a second polymorph that no 2002 entrant had found.

principles.name: Fresh items each round, key holder stays out
principles.plain: Standing schemes stay honest by making new items every round, releasing the truth only after closing, limiting entries, hiding entrant identities, and keeping the person who holds the key out of the contest.
principles.how_to_check: Is there a written rule for each of: item retirement once truth is released; who holds the key and that they do not enter; entries allowed per entrant per round; entrant codes instead of names; nothing in file names or metadata that leaks the recipe? Any missing rule, fail.
principles.why_it_matters_here: L2 is a hidden exam, and the plan already noticed file names spell out the recipe. The human contest allows one entry per organisation every two years. A machine exam that re-uses the same hidden items and accepts repeated submissions leaks its key through the scores. The metrology fix is new physical items each round, which has a real cost in powders and instrument time. That cost should be in the L2 sizing.

sources.title: The Reynolds Cup (rules and guidelines page)
sources.what_it_says: Biennial. New mixtures each round, made and judged by the previous winner, who therefore does not compete. One entry per organisation. True compositions released after all entries are in. Anonymous ranking; only the top three are named.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 17043:2023 Conformity assessment: general requirements for the competence of proficiency testing providers
sources.what_it_says: From memory, not opened (ISO site blocked the fetcher; URL from memory): requires confidentiality of participant identity, measures against collusion and falsification, and documented item preparation, homogeneity and stability.

sources.title: The International Harmonized Protocol for the proficiency testing of analytical chemistry laboratories
sources.what_it_says: Search result and memory only: rounds are repeated with fresh materials; assigned values are disclosed after the deadline; participants are identified by code.

prior_art.name: Reynolds Cup (Clay Minerals Society)
prior_art.what_it_is: A free, biennial, blind contest since 2002. Three weighed mineral mixtures per round, about 100 sample sets, no phase list given, any method allowed. Score is the sum of absolute wt% errors; ties inside the key's uncertainty go to tie-breaks that count missed and wrongly named phases. Truth released after closing. 448 participants and about 14,000 analyses over 2002-2014.
prior_art.overlaps_which_item: L2 (hidden-recipe exam on weighed mixtures); D4 (tie rule); N1/D1 (grouping levels fixed in advance); G17/G20 in gaps.md
prior_art.what_is_left_open: It is for human analysts, on clay-bearing rocks, three items every two years, one entry per organisation. No machine-facing submission or public scoring code was seen. Not inorganic-synthesis chemistry. New to the notes: the rules detail (purity within 1 wt%, XRD+XRF split checks, published grouping spreadsheet, tie-break inside key uncertainty, organiser does not compete).

prior_art.name: Past Reynolds Cup mixtures on sale
prior_art.what_it_is: The society's store lists past contest reference mixtures at $250 per unit, 2-4 g each, limit of 4 units, several past rounds listed.
prior_art.overlaps_which_item: plan.md DON'T DO row (buying past contest powders on one unverified price); G20
prior_art.what_is_left_open: The price is now verified on the seller's own page, so 'unverified' can be dropped. The don't-buy call still stands for a different reason: few items, clay-heavy, and their compositions were released to entrants after each round, so they are not hidden. Whether full keys are posted publicly was not checked.

prior_art.name: Butler and Hillier 2021, automated full-pattern summation (R package powdR) scored on Reynolds Cup samples
prior_art.what_it_is: An automatic algorithm that picks the phases itself from a 201-pattern library, run on 27 samples from nine past contests. Mean absolute error 0.57 wt% for non-clay minerals, 2.37 for clays, 4.43 for non-crystalline phases. Would have placed in the top three in all nine contests.
prior_art.overlaps_which_item: L2 novelty claim (machine-scored on blind-contest weighed mixtures); N3 (practice exam); G20 conclusion
prior_art.what_is_left_open: Abstract only was read. It is a one-off, run by the tool's authors after the truth was public, with their own library, on minerals, scored on amounts not on naming. It shows 'a machine scored against contest weighed mixtures' already exists. It does not give a standing, hidden, third-party exam.

prior_art.name: Lutterotti et al. 2019, full-profile search-match (FPSM) tested on round-robin scans
prior_art.what_it_is: A fully automatic phase-naming and quantifying tool with a public web form, tested on IUCr round-robin data set 1h (within 2% absolute of weighed values) and on all four samples of the 2002 search-match round robin. One sample failed because the structure was not in the open database; on another the tool disagreed with the organisers' key.
prior_art.overlaps_which_item: N3 and D6 (re-using public round-robin scans as a machine practice exam); P12 positive control; G14/G17
prior_art.what_is_left_open: Five scans, authors' own run, no written marking rule, no repeat. Confirms the round-robin scans were publicly downloadable from the IUCr site in 2019 and have already been used as development examples, so they are contaminated as an unseen test.

prior_art.name: IUCr CPD round robin on quantitative phase analysis (Madsen 2001; Scarlett 2002)
prior_art.what_it_is: 1998-2002 interlaboratory test. Eight three-phase weighed mixtures plus samples built to trigger preferred orientation, non-crystalline content and microabsorption, a 7-phase synthetic bauxite, a natural rock with no key, and two drug mixtures. Key cross-checked by XRF. Separate arms for supplied scans and own scans. Scored with a concentration-weighted Kullback-Leibler distance.
prior_art.overlaps_which_item: D6 and N3 (harder public weighed sets); G20; L2 design
prior_art.what_is_left_open: New to the notes: phase identities were GIVEN to entrants, so it never tested naming; weighed values have been public since 1999; only the supplied-data arm is a fixed scan set; roughly 20 scans in total. Usable as a positive control and a small practice set, not as a hidden exam.

prior_art.name: Search-Match Round Robin 2002 (Le Meins, Cranswick, Le Bail)
prior_art.what_it_is: The only phase-NAMING round robin found. Four real samples, two steps (without and with chemistry), about 25-30 entrants, nine software packages. One entrant found all ten phases. Grading was lenient and done by hand: same-series members were accepted.
prior_art.overlaps_which_item: D1 and N1 (marking rule, 'same family' tier); G14
prior_art.what_is_left_open: New detail: database age alone failed about 16% of entrants on one sample; one phase was missing from the database; the key was later challenged (see FPSM 2019). No written rule card, four items, and no repeat round was found (one search; absence not proven).

prior_art.name: León-Reina et al. 2016 spiking series and its Zenodo record
prior_art.what_it_is: 78 careful analyses of mixtures spiked with 0.12 to 4.0 wt% of a minor phase (inorganic, organic and glass series), lab Cu and Mo sources plus synchrotron. Record is CC BY 4.0, about 4.8 MB, raw scans in vendor formats (.raw, .xrdml) and .XY.
prior_art.overlaps_which_item: D6 (one of the three harder public sets); N3 wt% bands; G20; G28
prior_art.what_is_left_open: Landing page and paper abstract only; nothing downloaded. Licence and size are now verified. Much of the range sits near the physical detection floor (about 0.2 wt%; good accuracy only above 1 wt%), and phase identities are known by design, so it measures a detection curve, not open naming. Vendor formats need conversion.

prior_art.name: Szymanski et al. 2023, 240 two-phase mixtures
prior_art.what_it_is: Measured two-phase mixtures from eight compounds in two lithium oxide chemical families, minority phase 2 to 20 wt%, from an adaptive-scanning paper in npj Computational Materials.
prior_art.overlaps_which_item: D6; N3 (only its under-10 wt% band counts as harder)
prior_art.what_is_left_open: Search-result snippet only in this run; the article page redirects to a sign-in flow for the fetcher and was not followed. Where the raw scans live, their size and licence were not confirmed here. Correction 26 in plan.md (public raw scans supported for one of three sets) still stands.

prior_art.name: NIST reference materials and ASTM C1365 qualification
prior_art.what_it_is: SRM 676a is a certified alumina powder (99.02% +/- 1.11% crystalline) for anchoring quantitative powder XRD. SRM 2686, 2687, 2688 and 2686a are certified cement clinkers. ASTM C1365 makes a lab qualify its method against them within per-phase precision limits.
prior_art.overlaps_which_item: L2 (how a partner lab and method get qualified); P12 positive control; builds.md mention of SRM 2686a
prior_art.what_is_left_open: SRM 2686a is in the notes; SRM 676a and ASTM C1365 are not. Cement only, amounts only, human labs. The ASTM text itself was not opened (paywalled). Shows the qualify-against-a-certified-item pattern; does not cover naming or ML tools.

prior_art.name: ISO 13528, ISO/IEC 17043 and the IUPAC Harmonized Protocol
prior_art.what_it_is: The standard rule books for proficiency tests: how to set the assigned value and its uncertainty, homogeneity and stability limits (0.3 of the scoring SD), z and z-prime scores, confidentiality, anti-collusion.
prior_art.overlaps_which_item: D4 (tie function); L2 design; G18 (the notes already apply z-prime to the thermoelectric side)
prior_art.what_is_left_open: Standards were not opened (ISO and IUPAC pages blocked the fetcher); a secondary explainer of the homogeneity rule was opened. The notes use these for thermoelectric numbers only, not for XRD. They are written for numeric results. From memory, ISO 13528 has a short clause on qualitative results, but I know of no standard score for a multi-label phase list. That scoring rule is genuinely open.

prior_art.name: Lima-de-Faria et al. 1990 tiers, and Allmann and Hinek 2007 ICSD structure types
prior_art.what_it_is: 1990: the IUCr definitions of four structure-similarity tiers. 2007: the stepwise, rule-based procedure ICSD uses to assign entries to structure types (space group, Wyckoff sequence, Pearson symbol, axis-ratio and angle ranges, formula type, required or forbidden elements).
prior_art.overlaps_which_item: N1 (tiered marker); D1 (tricky pairs and guard rows); G14
prior_art.what_is_left_open: The 1990 paper is in the notes; the 2007 ICSD procedure is not. The 1990 text leaves tolerances to the user and says so. The 2007 rules are published but the assignments live inside a licensed database; whether an open implementation exists is unknown to me. A free, installable marker with declared tolerances still looks open.

prior_art.name: GALAXI (arXiv 2609.06908, Sept 2026)
prior_art.what_it_is: A new ML phase-naming system: one yes/no classifier per structure for 64,594 open-database structures, followed by refinement. Reports micro-F1 0.935 on a curated set of measured scans and a public web interface.
prior_art.overlaps_which_item: N3 (another tool to run beside Dara); L2 (a likely entrant); G20 (are known-answer sets too easy)
prior_art.what_is_left_open: Abstract only; the HTML full text returned 404. The abstract does not say where the test scans came from, how many there are, or what counted as a correct phase. That is the exact gap a published marking rule would fill. Read the full paper before citing the number.

prior_art.name: León-Reina et al. 2009 round robin on Rietveld analysis of Portland cements
prior_art.what_it_is: A domain-specific interlaboratory test of quantitative XRD on cements (J. Appl. Cryst. 42).
prior_art.overlaps_which_item: L2 (shows domain round robins exist beyond clays and the IUCr set)
prior_art.what_is_left_open: Seen as a search result and recalled from memory only; details not verified. Listed so stage 2 can check it. Human labs, amounts only.

measurement-science.notes:
ANSWER TO THE USER'S QUESTION, THIS LENS ONLY. Yes, this is eval work, and an older field has done the physical version of it for 25 years. The plan already matches that practice in five places: a tie rule (D4), a 'cannot tell' verdict with guard rows (D1), wt% bands fixed in advance and a 'truth in candidate list' flag (N3), calling public-answer sets a practice exam, and labelling L2 a one-instrument exam. Keep all five.

WHAT A PRACTISING DIFFRACTION PERSON WOULD FIND NAIVE (ranked). (1) Treating the weighed recipe as truth with no ingredient-purity scan, no independent chemistry check and no error bar (P2). (2) A noise ladder as the main difficulty axis; the real breakers are systematic: grain shading (microabsorption), grains lying flat (preferred orientation), peak overlap, poor crystallinity, mixed-composition phases (P6). (3) Re-using the IUCr quantification scans as a naming exam without saying the original entrants were told the phases (P1). (4) Treating misses below about 1 wt% as tool failures (P7). (5) Treating 'cannot tell' as a property of the pair only; it also depends on scan quality (P9). (6) Assuming a published key is final; one 2002 key was contradicted in 2019 (P13). (7) Reading 'one lab' results as general (P5). (8) Hand-mixing hundreds of small powders with no homogeneity or stability check (P4). (9) A standing hidden exam on the same items with unlimited machine submissions (P14). (10) Not stating whether the element list is given, when in real use it always is (P10).

HOW MUCH OF THE LONG-TERM AIM ALREADY EXISTS. Existing pieces: a blind weighed-mixture contest with fresh items and released truth (Reynolds Cup, human, minerals); a public verified weighed scan set (IUCr CPD, truth public since 1999, identities given); one naming round robin (2002, four real samples, hand-graded); machines already scored post hoc on both contest sets (FPSM 2019; powdR 2021, top-three in nine contests); the statistics rule books (ISO 13528, IUPAC). Not found: a standing, hidden, machine-facing, naming-first exam on inorganic-synthesis mixtures with a published marking rule and a multi-label score. Two web searches found none; that is absence of evidence, not proof. So G20's 'novelty is narrow' is right and should be narrowed one step further: 'machine scored on contest weighed mixtures' is NOT new; 'standing + hidden + third-party + naming-first + synthesis chemistry + written marking rule' still appears open. Out of our reach without a lab: fresh physical items each round, XRF checks, second-instrument subset.

CHEAPEST NEW ACTIONS THIS LENS SUGGESTS (all web-only or tiny, each download needs the user's yes): run the pipeline once on IUCr sample 1 supplied scans as a positive control (P12); add a key-error input to the tie function (P3); add false-positive count and single-phase trap items (P8); write the grouping table with numeric tolerances before scoring the 40 rows (P9).

CORRECTIONS TO THE NOTES. The $250 Reynolds Cup unit price is now verified on the seller's page. Not in gaps.md or plan.md before this run: Butler and Hillier 2021, Lutterotti 2019, Allmann and Hinek 2007, SRM 676a, ASTM C1365, GALAXI, the fact that the IUCr round robin supplied phase identities, its XRF-verified key, its supplied-data arm and its Kullback-Leibler score. In the notes but not re-opened here: XRDBench, Codabench, RADAR-PD, Doebelin 2020, AIF. XMatcher (arXiv 2607.17162, abstract read) is a tool with no test set or marking rule, so it is not prior art for the eval.

SOURCE HONESTY. opened=true means I loaded that URL in this run and it says what I state; for Springer and two IUCr items only the abstract was readable. opened=false items (ISO 13528, ISO/IEC 17043, IUPAC protocol, Eurachem guide, Brindley 1945, Szymanski 2023, León-Reina 2009) rest on memory or search snippets; the two ISO URLs and the Brindley DOI are from memory and unverified.
